etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Borrowed from Middle French impulser, from Latin impulsus.

For spelling, as in pulse, the -e (on -lse) is so the end is pronounced /ls/, rather than /lz/ as in pulls, and does not change the vowel (‘u’). Compare else, false, convulse.

definitions.definition: A thrust; a push; a sudden force that impels.

quote.citation: c. 1715-1716, Samuel Clarke, letter to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
quote.text: All spontaneous animal motion is performed by mechanical impulse.

definitions.definition: A wish or urge, particularly a sudden one prompting action.

quote.citation: 1685, John Dryden, transl., “Preface”, in Sylvæ: Or, The Second Part of Poetical Miscellanies, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC; reprinted Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, page 16:
quote.text: Theſe were my natural Impulses for the undertaking:  […]

quote.citation: 1907 January, Harold Bindloss, chapter 20, in The Dust of Conflict, 1st Canadian edition, Toronto, Ont.: McLeod & Allen, →OCLC:
quote.text: Tony's face expressed relief, and Nettie sat silent for a moment until the vicar said “It was a generous impulse, but it may have been a momentary one, […] .”

quote.citation: 1930, Norman Lindsay, Redheap, Sydney, N.S.W.: Ure Smith, published 1965, →OCLC, page 218:
quote.text: An impulse urged him to plant a sudden blow on it, by he forced himself to consider the impolicy of such an act.

definitions.definition: (physics) The integral of force over time.

quote.citation: 1614, Walter Ralegh [i.e., Walter Raleigh], The Historie of the World […], London:  […]  William Stansby for Walter Burre, […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=1 to 5):
quote.text: With that force so impulsed and prest they are carried under the deepe Ocean.
